brief.intro: An apartment building is a multi-unit residential building — typically five to fifteen storeys — where every unit above the ground floor repeats the same layout, served by shared cores (stairs, lifts) and vertical risers running the full height. Unlike a single house, the planning problem is not one complex build but the same build repeated many times: the programme lives or dies on how fast and how consistently the typical-floor cycle runs, and on how smoothly the finishing trades move from unit to unit behind it. Structure is usually straightforward reinforced concrete, so the schedule risk sits in coordinating many trades through the same shafts and in keeping the finishing wave from stalling on any one floor. A well-run apartment building schedule reads like a production line: steady floor cycle time, then a disciplined trade train — waterproofing, tiling, second-fix MEP, snagging — moving continuously upward.

must_get_right: Lock the typical-floor cycle time early — it sets the pace for every trade behind it.
Protect the riser/shaft sequence — once a floor's risers are cast in, no unit above can finish without a clear, tested stack.
Waterproof wet areas and test before tiling — this is the single biggest source of rework and handover defects.
Plan finishing as a moving wave, not a floor-by-floor stop — trades should flow continuously unit to unit.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and civil run a 6-day working calendar. Finishing and MEP trades may move to an extended day or a second shift at peak to protect the handover date. A weather allowance is embedded in the civil calendar where relevant.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The typical-floor structural cycle sets the earliest date each floor's finishing can start. Once structure has run several floors ahead of finishing, the true driving path transfers to the internal finishing sequence — wet-area waterproofing → screed/tiling → second-fix MEP → snagging — which is usually the real critical path from that point to handover, not the structural cycle itself.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen per typical floor before the cycle starts; a sample/mock-up unit is inspected and approved before the layout is repeated; a single mobilisation; and handover proceeds in floor-bands aligned with sales or occupancy readiness. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Tower crane and material-hoist time is shared across structure, envelope and MEP deliveries; riser sequencing restricts trade order within a floor; unit access must be coordinated with the sales/handover team as floor-bands complete; noise and working-hour limits often apply near occupied neighbours.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: floor-cycle slippage compounding across the tower, wet-area waterproofing failures forcing rework, and lift delivery delay blocking upper-floor fit-out access. Contingency is held at the structure-to-finishing transition and before final handover rather than spread thinly across floors.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (phase/floor-band summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 (floor-by-floor); expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead by unit/trade for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
